extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy/literary theory and writers/critics of comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical/critical criteria for what makes things laughable and how laughter functions socially and aesthetically. Extracts Bergson's diagnostic principles and examples for analyzing comic effects in form, movement, situation, words, and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic is strictly human
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic does not exist outside the pale of what is strictly human; you may laugh at an animal or an object only because you detect some human attitude, expression, shape or use in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: you laugh at an animal only for its human attitude; you laugh at a hat not for felt or straw but for the human caprice whose mould it assumes. Anti-pattern: treating landscapes or non-human phenomena as intrinsically laughable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter requires emotional indifference (momentary anesthesia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter usually accompanies an absence of feeling; the comic demands something like a momentary anesthesia of the heart — emotion is the enemy of comic effect, which appeals to intelligence rather than sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: to experience or present comic effect, spectators must be disinterested rather than emotionally involved. Example: a moving drama becomes comic if sympathy is suspended. Anti-pattern: trying to make people laugh out of scenes charged with active pity or sorrow without creating emotional distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter is social and needs an echo
rubrics_metrics.description: Our laughter is always the laughter of a group; laughter appears to need an echo — it reverberates among other intelligences and often depends on shared customs and ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: fuller theatres cause more uncontrolled laughter; many comic effects fail in translation because they rely on group-specific customs. Production note: comic material may be audience-dependent; solitary presentation may fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter has a social/corrective function
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter answers requirements of life in common and has a social signification: it acts as a corrective gesture to restrain eccentricity and inelasticity in character, mind or body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: treat laughter as a social sanction — it intimidates by humiliating and helps maintain sociability and adaptability. Anti-pattern: reading laughter solely as aesthetic amusement without social utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic arises from mechanical rigidity / inelasticity / automatism
rubrics_metrics.description: The laughable element often consists in a certain mechanical inelasticity — a lack of adaptability where living pliableness is expected (e.g., a runner who falls, a victim of a practical joke, stereotyped actions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: stumbling, continuing the same movement despite changed circumstances, or acting like a machine. Production note: emphasize mismatch between situation and inflexible response to produce comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absentmindedness (lagging behind the present) as source of comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Absentmindedness—thinking of what one has done rather than what one is doing, or living in a past/imaginary situation—produces comic effects by revealing an inner automaticity and failure to adapt to present reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Don Quixote walking like a somnambulist; systematic absentmindedness organized around one central idea yields cumulative comic effects. Anti-pattern: confusing simple awkwardness with sustained absentminded character without visible causal history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law: the more natural the cause, the more comic the effect
rubrics_metrics.description: When a comic effect originates in a cause that seems natural or intelligible, the effect is more comic; watching absentmindedness develop before us is funnier than seeing it presented as an isolated fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application: in comedic construction, show the genesis or growth of the oddity rather than presenting it as an arbitrary joke. Example: an absentmindedness that grows from reading romances becomes funnier as its cause is traced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deformity becomes comic if it can be imitated by a normally built person
rubrics_metrics.description: A deformity that may become comic is one that a normally built person could successfully imitate; laughable deformity suggests a pose or habit that normal people could adopt (e.g., a hunchback suggesting holding oneself badly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use in caricature and physical comedy: if an audience can mentally or physically mimic the deformity, it is more likely to be comic. Anti-pattern: deformities that are wholly other, inscrutable or impossible to simulate do not produce comic effect (they may elicit pity or horror instead).

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughable facial expression = fixed, permanent grimace (stereotypy)
rubrics_metrics.description: A laughable expression is one that promises nothing more than it gives — a unique and permanent grimace implying that the person's moral life has crystallized into a single cast of features; it suggests rigidity where mobility is expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish expressive beauty (stable but mobile) from comic fixity (stable and immobile). In performance/characterization, create faces/expressions that read as stereotyped automatism to heighten comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caricature: exaggeration of latent tendencies, not pure excess
rubrics_metrics.description: The caricaturist detects imperceptible tendencies in a face or form and magnifies them so that the model grimaces as it might in extremity; exaggeration must serve to reveal a distortion already implied by nature rather than be an aim in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance for artists/writers: exaggerate in the direction suggested by the subject's latent inclination (respect the ground plan) so that exaggeration appears as the subject completing its own grimace. Anti-pattern: arbitrary or aimless distortion that does not reveal an underlying tendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form as outline of movement; comic in forms that suggest arrested movement
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms are perceived as outlines of movements; comic forms are those that suggest the imprint of some stereotyped mechanical action or arrested movement (matter resisting the soul's mobility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical: look for physical forms that imply an arrested or repetitive action (a mouth that seems always to be laughing, a face always weeping). In staging/visual comedy, freeze or repeat movements to make form read as mechanical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic in reasoning/words: play upon ideas and relaxation of logic (dream-logic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic reasoning is a relaxation of the rules of reasoning: false argumentation that could be accepted in a dream, abbreviated reasonings (witticisms), play on words and sounds where meaning fades and sound predominates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: jokes that present only beginning and end of a reasoning; scenes where whispered phrases devolve into nonsense; gradual drift toward absurdity. Writing/performing tip: exploit dreamlike associative logic and sound-word play to create comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic in character: vices brought from without (ready-made rigidity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A vice that makes us laugh is one that is brought from without — a ready-made frame that lends its rigidity to the person rather than being fully incorporated; comic character retains an independent, visible 'vice' that operates like a puppet-master.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish tragic vices (deeply integrated) from comic vices (external, simplifying, stereotype-like). Character construction: present vices as externally imposed habits or frames that simplify the person and make them unconscious of themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic character is unconscious of being comic
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic person is generally comic in proportion to his ignorance of himself; as soon as he feels himself ridiculous he will change — the unconscious automatism is essential to the comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance note: keep the character unaware of the audience's ridicule; awareness often dissipates the comic effect. Example: Harpagon might alter behavior if he saw himself laughed at, showing why unconsciousness matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of resemblance/analogy: secondary forms borrow comedy from primary types
rubrics_metrics.description: Given one form of the laughable, other forms lacking the same comic essence become laughable by outward resemblance to the first; many comic effects are amusing because they recall a primary laughable type (e.g., dreamlike motifs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical implication: classify comic effects by their resemblance to prototype types (mechanical rigidity, absentmindedness, caricature, dream-logic). Creation tip: borrow recognizable primary comic patterns so variants register quickly with audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter is not necessarily benevolent or just
rubrics_metrics.description: Though laughter can have a useful corrective function, it is not always kind or equitable; it operates spontaneously and may punish the innocent while sparing the guilty — it is a natural, not a reflective, mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical caution: when using laughter or satire as corrective, be aware of its capacity for cruelty and injustice; comic creators should consider ethical effects though laughter itself is not reflective justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic provides relief and plays with tension (relaxation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic absurdity gives the impression of playing with ideas and relieves us from the strain of thinking; it invites temporary relaxation from the continuous effort of common sense and the tension of social living.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application: structure comic sequences to permit audience relaxation — progressive drift, crescendo to absurdity, repetition and playfulness invite shared relief. Balance corrective and relief functions for richer comic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic requires a neutral zone outside struggle and emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic appears within a neutral zone outside the sphere of strong emotion and struggle, where man exposes himself to others' curiosity; the comic is the rigidity left after serious life-penalties are excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive use: when analyzing or staging comedy, situate comic incidents where stakes are low enough to permit ridicule without moral harm. Anti-pattern: treating deeply tragic or high-stakes situations as comic without establishing neutrality.
